newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares end down as political crisis deepens.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares end down as political crisis deepens.

text.p: Bombay shares ended lower in jittery trade on Monday as uncertainty over the country's political picture mounted in the run-up to this week's confidence vote against the government, traders said.
They said domestic and foreign funds remained on the sidelines in low-volume trade.
"The uncertainty is increasing rather than decreasing," said Subra Subramanian, director at securities firm H.G. Asia. "This weekend has not helped much."

Congress party President Sitaram Kesri, who sparked a political crisis on March 30 when he abruptly withdrew his party's make-or-break support to the United Front's 10-month-old minority government, launched a scathing attack on Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda over the weekend.
Kesri told supporters on Saturday that although he did not hold a "grudge" against the ruling coalition, he viewed Deve Gowda as "not only inefficient but communal".
Analysts said the political uncertainty would keep cautious investors on the sidelines this week.
"Things are so much in the air -- the market will trade in a dead zone this week," the chief dealer at a U.K.-based brokerage said.

"I think we might see a period of low trading activity this week," said Himanshu Kaji, a member-broker of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). "The future course of the markets will depend on the crucial vote of confidence."
Shares of software firm Infosys Technologies hit a high of 1,359 rupees, before falling back to close a modest 7.25 rupees up at 1,250.
Traders said investors were buyers ahead of a bonus share issue due on Tuesday.
They said the market expected the firm to announce an issue of one bonus share for every one share held.
Infosys shares had gained 10 percent on Friday after the firm said it planned to issue bonus shares.

Shares of equipment-maker Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd (BHEL) rose 7.75 rupees, or 2.2 percent, to 365 as the stock attracted buying after the firm announced sharply improved results for 1996/97 last week.
State-run BHEL said last Thursday its net profit surged nearly 34 percent to 4.68 billion rupees ($130 million), from 3.5 billion in 1995/96.
Analysts said the results beat all market expectations with the average consensus net profit forecast pegged as low as 3.8 billion rupees.
